unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: This unit explores the different types of story writers create. You will meet five genres on the library shelves — adventure, mystery, fable, legend and realistic fiction — and learn the features that tell them apart. A courtroom story then shows realistic fiction at work, while twenty-five words built from the prefixes un-, dis- and in- and the endings -ible, -able and -ous stretch your vocabulary. Alongside this you will learn to link ideas smoothly with conjunctions and connective adverbs, and use them to write your own story opening.
unit.learningPath: Preview the genre goals and the twenty-five prefix words. Read both library tour passages, then both parts of the courtroom story. Answer the comprehension questions with evidence. Work through the six grammar sections on connectives. Sort and build words in the activities. Plan, draft and revise a story opening, then take feedback from a partner. Record the speaking tasks, complete the quiz and finish the self-assessment.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A situation where people are unhappy and may protest or cause trouble.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: There was unrest in the city because people wanted to change the rules.
practiceSentences: Weeks of unrest followed the decision, and the council finally agreed to listen.
The old tale described a kingdom full of unrest after the harvest failed.
What caused the unrest in the city described in our history book?
'Unfair rules often lead to unrest,' explained our teacher during the lesson.
I read about the unrest that ended when the leaders finally listened to the people.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - r - e - s - t
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me what unrest looks like in a community, then check my sentence about the old rule in this unit.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Feeling worried or uncomfortable about something.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: I felt uneasy when I heard a strange noise in the dark.
practiceSentences: An uneasy silence settled over the courtroom before the first speaker stood up.
Adam felt uneasy as the storm clouds gathered over the school field.
Do you feel uneasy when you have to speak in front of the class?
'Something about that creaking door makes me uneasy,' whispered Nora.
I was uneasy before my swimming test, but I felt fine once I started.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - e - a - s - y
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to describe a time I felt uneasy, and help me choose a stronger word if uneasy is too mild.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Something that happens suddenly and is not planned.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The rain was unexpected, so we got wet without our umbrellas.
practiceSentences: The best mysteries end with an unexpected twist that nobody saw coming.
An unexpected knock at the door made everyone look up from their books.
What was the most unexpected event in the story we read today?
'This unexpected gift is wonderful,' gasped Grandma, unwrapping the scarf.
Our picnic ended early because of an unexpected downpour of rain.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - e - x - p - e - c - t - e - d
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me how a writer uses an unexpected event to build suspense, then check my own example sentence.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not achieving the desired result or goal.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: He tried to climb the tree, but he was unsuccessful and fell down.
practiceSentences: Three unsuccessful attempts did not stop the team from trying once more.
The first rocket launch was unsuccessful, but the engineers refused to give up.
Why was the fox unsuccessful in catching the clever rabbit?
'My attempt at baking bread was unsuccessful,' admitted Dad, showing the flat loaf.
I was unsuccessful in my first spelling contest, so I practised even harder.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - s - u - c - c - e - s - s - f - u - l
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to explain how unsuccessful differs from incompetent, and listen to my two example sentences.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not known or recognised; something you have not seen before.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The new school was unfamiliar to me, so I felt a little nervous.
practiceSentences: Adventure stories often drop their heroes into unfamiliar places far from home.
Walking through the unfamiliar market, Sami held tightly to his father's hand.
How do you feel when you hear a completely unfamiliar language?
'These streets are unfamiliar to me,' admitted the taxi driver, checking his map.
On my first day at the new school, every corridor felt unfamiliar.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - f - a - m - i - l - i - a - r
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to describe somewhere unfamiliar using two senses, then tell me whether my description was clear.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not sure about something and not yet able to decide.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: I felt uncertain about which game to play.
practiceSentences: The witness sounded uncertain, so the lawyer asked the question again slowly.
The weather was uncertain, so we packed both sun hats and raincoats.
Are you still uncertain about which book to choose for your project?
'I'm uncertain whether this bridge is safe,' said the explorer, testing the ropes.
I felt uncertain about the last answer, so I checked my working twice.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - c - e - r - t - a - i - n
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me when it is sensible to say I am uncertain, and check that my sentence sounds honest rather than weak.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not knowing or realising something.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She was unaware that her friend needed help.
practiceSentences: Many families stayed unaware of the rule until the newspapers finally reported it.
The sleeping cat was unaware that a mouse was tiptoeing past its tail.
Were you unaware that the library closes early on Fridays?
'I was completely unaware of the surprise party,' laughed Maya.
I walked around unaware that a leaf was stuck in my hair all morning.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - a - w - a - r - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me the difference between unaware and unconscious, because both prefixes mean not.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not awake and not aware of what is happening.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: After falling off his bike, he was unconscious and needed help.
practiceSentences: The paramedics worked quickly because the patient was still unconscious on the pavement.
The knight in the story lay unconscious until the healer arrived with her herbs.
What should you do if you find someone unconscious after an accident?
'Call for help immediately if a person is unconscious,' taught the first-aid nurse.
My uncle told us how a falling branch knocked a hiker unconscious for a minute.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - i - q - u - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me why unique takes a rather than an, then test me on two more words that start with a long u sound.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Used to say that something is sad or disappointing.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Unfortunately, it started to rain during our picnic.
practiceSentences: Unfortunately, nobody questioned the unfair rule for more than thirty long years.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - f - o - r - t - u - n - a - t - e - l - y
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to pair unfortunately with fortunately in one short paragraph about a rule that changed.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix dis- (meaning 'not', 'opposite of', or 'remove')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not happy or pleased with something.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She was dissatisfied with her test score because she wanted to do better.
practiceSentences: Readers felt dissatisfied with the ending because the mystery was never properly explained.
The customer looked dissatisfied because the shoes were the wrong size.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to compare dissatisfied with uneasy, since both name an uncomfortable feeling.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix dis- (meaning 'not', 'opposite of', or 'remove')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A situation that makes something harder or less good.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Not having a bike is a disadvantage when my friends ride to school.

Is being small always a disadvantage when you play basketball?
'Forgetting your ruler is a real disadvantage in a maths test,' warned Teacher Yasmin.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to name one disadvantage in the unit story, and check that I gave evidence from the text.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix dis- (meaning 'not', 'opposite of', or 'remove')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A condition that makes it harder for someone to do certain things.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Some people with a disability use a wheelchair to help them move around.
practiceSentences: The old rule in the story treated a disability as a reason to refuse a place.
A disability did not stop the athlete from winning three gold medals.
How can our school make sure a pupil with a disability can join every activity?

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: d - i - s - a - b - i - l - i - t - y
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me how a school can welcome every learner, and remind me to speak about people respectfully.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix dis- (meaning 'not', 'opposite of', or 'remove')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To ignore something or not pay attention to it.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: If you disregard the rules, you might get in trouble.
practiceSentences: Amal argued that the rule showed complete disregard for the students it affected.
Drivers who disregard the speed limit put everyone around them in danger.
Why did the character disregard the warning sign beside the river?
'Please don't disregard the instructions at the top of the worksheet,' reminded our teacher.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: d - i - s - r - e - g - a - r - d
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to use disregard as a verb and then as a noun, and tell me whether both sentences work.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix dis- (meaning 'not', 'opposite of', or 'remove')
dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Treating someone unfairly because of who they are.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: It is wrong to show discrimination against someone just because they are different.
practiceSentences: Laws exist to stop discrimination, yet people still have to notice it and speak up.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to spell discrimination one syllable at a time, then use it in a sentence about fairness.

dictionaryLinks.groupTitle: Words with the Prefix dis- (meaning 'not', 'opposite of', or 'remove')

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me how dismantle can describe both furniture and unfair rules, and check my two examples.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not finished or not having all the parts.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: i - n - c - o - m - p - l - e - t - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to strip the prefix from incomplete and build two more in- words the same way.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: When someone is treated unfairly or not given what they deserve.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: It is an injustice when some children do not have enough food to eat.
practiceSentences: Naming an injustice out loud is the first step towards putting it right.
The brave lawyer spent her whole life fighting injustice in the courts.
What injustice did the main character face at the start of the story?
'Staying silent about injustice only helps it grow,' said the guest speaker.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: i - n - j - u - s - t - i - c - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me how injustice and discrimination are connected, and check that my explanation stays clear.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not able to do something.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: i - n - c - a - p - a - b - l - e

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not able to do something well or correctly.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: He felt incompetent when he could not solve the maths problem.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to explain the difference between incapable and incompetent using one example each.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Unable to be defeated or overcome; very strong.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The superhero felt invincible when he saved the city from danger.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: i - n - v - i - n - c - i - b - l - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me what Amal means when she says even a law that seems invincible can fall.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Hard to read or not clear enough to understand.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: My teacher said my handwriting was illegible, so I need to write more neatly.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: i - l - l - e - g - i - b - l - e

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Able to be travelled on or through, especially by boats.

readings.title: The Library Tour: Adventure and Mystery
readings.setting: A school library and a small town courthouse
readings.passageScript:
"Welcome to our school library," said Teacher Yasmin, spreading her arms wide. She stood in front of five colourful bookshelves, and each one carried its own banner. "Today we are not walking through the library. Instead, we are travelling through the world of story genres. A genre is simply a type or kind of story. Each shelf holds one genre, and by the end of the tour you will know which shelf to visit."
She walked to the first shelf, which showed a bright orange banner with a compass and a map. "This is our adventure shelf," she said. "Adventure stories take characters on exciting journeys. The characters face danger, solve problems and discover new places. Picture a young sailor crossing the open sea during a terrible storm. Picture three friends climbing the northern highlands to find a hidden waterfall. In adventure writing the setting changes often, and the plot is full of action. The main character is usually brave, although she may feel afraid at first. Adventure stories keep you turning the pages, because you always want to know what happens next."
Teacher Yasmin moved to the second shelf. Its banner was dark blue and covered with magnifying glasses and question marks. "This is the mystery shelf," she explained. "In mystery writing something puzzling happens at the very beginning, and the characters spend the rest of the story working it out. Perhaps a valuable book has vanished from the library. Perhaps a strange light appears on the beach every Thursday night. Mystery stories are built on suspense. The writer gives you real clues, but also plants false clues to keep you guessing. A good mystery makes you feel like a detective, and the ending suddenly makes everything make sense."

readings.title: The Library Tour: Fable, Legend and Realistic Fiction
readings.setting: A school library and a small town courthouse
readings.passageScript:
The third shelf carried a green banner showing animals dressed in human clothes. "Here is our fable shelf," said Teacher Yasmin, smiling. "Fables are short stories, and animals are usually the main characters. The animals talk, think and behave like people. Every fable teaches a moral, which is a lesson about how to live well. You may know the fable of the lion and the mouse, which shows that even the smallest creature can help the mightiest. There is also the tale of the patient fox who outwits the hyena by thinking instead of fighting. Fables have been told for thousands of years, because their lessons never grow old."
She pointed to the fourth shelf, which carried a golden banner decorated with stars and mountains. "This is our legend shelf," she continued. "Legends are traditional stories passed down through many generations. They are often set in the distant past, and their heroes perform extraordinary deeds. Some legends explain how a river was carved or how a mountain first rose. Legends differ from fables because they do not always end with a clear moral. Instead they celebrate courage, wisdom and the history of a whole community."
Finally Teacher Yasmin reached the fifth shelf. Its banner was calm sky blue, showing schoolbags, bicycles and houses. "The last genre is realistic fiction," she said. "These stories are invented, yet they feel as though they could really happen. The characters are ordinary people in ordinary situations, such as moving house or learning to get along with a younger sister. Realistic fiction helps us understand other people's feelings, rather like looking through a window into someone else's life. There are no dragons and no magic here, but this genre can be as powerful as any other."
She looked at the class and smiled. "Now you know the five shelves. A good reader tries many genres, so keep reading and keep exploring."

readings.title: The Case of the Incomplete Rule, part 1
readings.setting: A school library and a small town courthouse
readings.passageScript:
The morning air in Bukoba town felt heavy, and clouds hovered like thoughts waiting to fall. Inside the small red-brick courthouse, children from Liberty Primary School took their seats. They were there for a role-play trial, part of their civic education week.
Amal straightened her papers. "I am the lawyer," she whispered to Sami, who was playing the judge. "Let us make this trial meaningful."
"It already is," Sami answered. "We are discussing a real law that was dismantled last year, one that caused a lot of discrimination."
As the pretend trial began, the room grew quiet. Their teacher read from an old dusty file: "This rule denied students with a disability a place at the top schools unless they passed a different exam."
Gasps filled the room. Amal stood up. "This is not only unfair. It is injustice," she said firmly. "The rule shows clear disregard for fairness."
"Objection!" called Nora, the pretend prosecutor. "This law was never created to harm anyone."
"But it did harm people," Amal replied. "Ask any student who felt unwelcome, uneasy, or ignored."
After the trial the students gathered in the library. "We need to understand how these rules were made," said Sami.
They opened old files from the education office. Some were illegible, written in ink that had faded to grey. Others were crowded with stamps and long paragraphs.
"Look at this one," said Nora. "It is full of crossed-out sections, so it is clearly incomplete."
Sami pointed to a line. "And this part says the rule was reviewed during a time of civil unrest."
They turned the pages, curious and focused. Then Amal stopped at a folder marked 'Unheard Voices'.
Inside were letters from students across the country. One line read: "I feel as though I am being punished for a condition I cannot change."
"That is heartbreaking," whispered Nora.
Amal sat down slowly. "These students never had a chance to speak in court, did they?"

readings.title: The Case of the Incomplete Rule, part 2
readings.setting: A school library and a small town courthouse
readings.passageScript:
Sami shook his head. "They wrote letters instead of giving speeches."
"Perhaps they believed that nobody would listen," Nora added.
"We are listening now," said Amal, her voice firm. "And that matters."
The group fell quiet again, not from sadness but from understanding. They were not simply reading; they were witnessing something that should never have been forgotten.
"That rule did not only block schools," Sami said at last. "It blocked hope."
Later that day their teacher led a group discussion. "Why do you think this law lasted so long?" she asked.
"Because many people were unaware of its effects," said Sami.
"Because some were too uncertain to speak," added Nora.
Amal raised her hand. "And some felt incapable of changing the system."
"That is a powerful reflection," the teacher said. "So what finally helped to change it?"
"Voices," said Amal. "Letters. Stories."
The next day it rained hard and the power flickered, yet the students worked on by window light. They were building a timeline of events.
"This part shows when the law was passed," said Sami.
"And this is when the protests began," added Nora.
Amal drew a set of scales. "This stands for the fairness we must protect, even when the work feels monotonous or slow."
Nora grinned. "Your drawing is as clear as a gavel's knock."
"And your timeline is as navigable as a city map," said Amal.
At the end of the week the school held a debate. Amal opened her notes. "This law caused disadvantage," she said. "It may have been legal, but it was not just."
Nora stood. "Unfortunately," she began, "we did not fix it sooner. Fortunately, we are speaking now."
The headteacher had watched in silence, and now she rose. "You have reminded us of something important. Old laws are not always right. Some must be questioned, and some must be changed."
She read the slogan on their board: "Unfairness, once noticed, must be challenged."
That evening Amal wrote in her journal: "The court was pretend, but the feeling was real. If we stay silent, silence wins. If we speak together, even a law that seems invincible can fall."

grammar.title: What Are Connectives and Conjunctions?
grammar.explanation: A connective is any word or phrase that links ideas across your writing. A conjunction is one kind of connective, and it joins words, phrases or clauses inside a single sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Connectives glue ideas together so the reader can follow your thinking.
Without connectives the writing is choppy: "The rule was unfair. The students protested. The rule was changed."
With connectives it flows: "The rule was unfair, so the students protested, and eventually it was changed."
Three families do this work in English.
Coordinating conjunctions join two equal ideas inside one sentence: and, but, so.
Subordinating conjunctions hang the smaller idea onto the bigger one: because, although, when.
Connective adverbs link one whole sentence to the next: however, therefore, meanwhile.
Every connective carries a job — adding, contrasting, giving a reason, or showing time.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often string every idea together with "and", so the whole paragraph turns into one breathless sentence. Choose the connective that names the real relationship instead: "but" for contrast, "so" for a result, "because" for a reason.
grammar.memoryTip: Say the two ideas aloud, then ask yourself one question: am I adding, contrasting, explaining or timing? The answer names the family you need.
grammar.practice: Part A. Name the family of each connective in bold: coordinating, subordinating or connective adverb. | The files were dusty, but the students kept reading. | Although the ink had faded, Amal found the date. | The room fell silent. However, nobody left. | Part B. Rewrite each choppy pair as one smooth sentence, using any connective you like. | The law was old. Nobody had questioned it. | The rain fell hard. The students worked by window light. | Nora wanted to speak. She stood up. | Part C. Explain in one sentence why good writing needs more connectives than just "and". || Answer Key (for self-checking) — Part A: 1) "but" = coordinating conjunction; 2) "Although" = subordinating conjunction; 3) "However" = connective adverb. Part B is open-ended (many smooth combinations work) — model answers: "The law was old, but nobody had questioned it." / "The rain fell hard, so the students worked by window light." / "Nora wanted to speak, so she stood up." Part C is open-ended — model answer: "Good writing needs more than 'and' because different connectives show contrast, reasons, results and time, not just addition."

grammar.title: Coordinating Conjunctions (FANBOYS)
grammar.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions join two ideas of equal importance. There are seven of them, they spell the word FANBOYS, and each one does a slightly different job.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
For gives a reason and sounds more formal than "because": "They worked hard, for they believed in justice."
And adds information: "Amal read the files and shared the letters."
Nor adds a second negative idea: "She did not complain, nor did she give up."
But shows contrast: "The law helped, but it was incomplete."
Or offers a choice: "You can write a letter or give a speech."
Yet shows surprising contrast: "The task was long, yet they finished on time."
So shows a result: "The rule was unjust, so it was dismantled."
Punctuation: put a comma before FANBOYS only when it joins two complete sentences.
Two complete ideas: "The trial began, and the room grew quiet."
One subject with two actions: "Amal read and shared the letters." No comma is needed there.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers drop the comma when FANBOYS joins two complete sentences, then add one when it joins only two verbs. Test it by covering the conjunction: if both halves could stand alone, the comma belongs.
grammar.memoryTip: Chant FANBOYS on seven fingers: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. Finger one gives the reason and finger seven gives the result; the middle five add, deny, contrast, choose and surprise.
grammar.practice: Part A. Choose the best FANBOYS word for each gap. | I wanted to help, ______ I did not know what to do. | You can come with us, ______ you can stay at home. | The students were tired, ______ they kept working. | She studied every day, ______ she wanted to pass the exam. | He did not read the notice, ______ did he ask about it. | They found old files, ______ many of them were illegible. | The rule was changed, ______ the students had spoken up. | Part B. Choose the better word from the brackets. | The hero wanted to cross the river, ______ there was no bridge. (but / and) | Would you like to read a mystery ______ a legend tonight? (or / yet) | The fable was short, ______ it taught an important lesson. (yet / for) | Maya finished her homework, ______ she went outside to play. (so / nor) | The children packed food ______ water for the long walk. (and / but) | Part C. Copy the two sentences from Part B that need no comma, and explain why. || Answer Key (for self-checking) — Part A: 1) but, 2) or, 3) yet, 4) for, 5) nor, 6) but (and is also acceptable), 7) for. Part B: 1) but, 2) or, 3) yet, 4) so, 5) and. Part C: sentences 2 ("Would you like to read a mystery or a legend tonight?") and 5 ("The children packed food and water for the long walk.") need no comma, because in each the conjunction joins two objects of a single verb rather than two complete sentences — covering the conjunction leaves a fragment, not two standalone sentences.

grammar.title: Subordinating Conjunctions
grammar.explanation: A subordinating conjunction joins the main clause to a subordinate clause. The subordinate clause carries extra information and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
because gives a reason: "They protested because the rule was unfair."
although and even though show contrast in spite of something: "Although it rained, they kept working."
when marks a point in time: "When the teacher asked, Amal raised her hand."
while shows two things happening together: "While Sami read, Nora took notes."
before shows what happened first: "Before the debate, they gathered evidence."
after shows what came next: "After the trial, they went to the library."
since means "because" or "from the time that": "Since she loved animals, she chose fables."
if sets a condition: "If we speak together, change is possible."
unless means "if not": "The rule stayed unless someone challenged it."
until marks a time limit: "They searched until they found the folder."
Punctuation: when the subordinate clause comes first, close it with a comma.
Subordinate clause first: "Because the rule was unfair, they protested."
Main clause first: "They protested because the rule was unfair." No comma is needed.
grammar.commonMistake: A subordinate clause written on its own is not yet a sentence. "Because it rained." leaves the reader waiting, so finish the thought: "Because it rained, they worked inside."
grammar.memoryTip: Picture the main clause as the trunk and the subordinate clause as the branch. The branch cannot stand without the trunk, and the branch placed first needs a comma to hold it on.
grammar.practice: Part A. Fill each gap with the best subordinating conjunction. | ______ the students found the letters, they felt heartbroken. | Amal spoke firmly ______ she believed in justice. | ______ it rained heavily, the students kept working by window light. | They could not read the documents ______ the ink had faded. | ______ you notice unfairness, you should speak up. | Sami searched the files ______ he found the folder marked Unheard Voices. | ______ the debate began, the headteacher sat in silence. | The law remained ______ brave students challenged it. | Part B. Use this box: because, although, when, if, unless, while, until, after, before, since. | ______ you enjoy exciting journeys, you should try an adventure story. | The detective did not give up ______ she found the missing jewel. | ______ the storm was fierce, the sailors kept the boat steady. | The children listened carefully ______ Teacher Yasmin told the legend. | You will not understand the moral ______ you read the whole fable. | ______ the story ended, everyone clapped. | He chose a mystery ______ he loved solving puzzles. | Part C. Rewrite three of your Part A answers so the subordinate clause moves to the front, and add the comma. || Answer Key (for self-checking) — Part A: 1) When, 2) because, 3) Although, 4) because, 5) If, 6) until, 7) Before, 8) until. Part B: 1) If, 2) until, 3) Although, 4) while, 5) unless, 6) After, 7) because. Part C: the exact wording is up to you, but pick any three Part A sentences whose subordinate clause was NOT already first — model rewrites: "Because she believed in justice, Amal spoke firmly." / "Because the ink had faded, they could not read the documents." / "Until he found the folder marked Unheard Voices, Sami searched the files." / "Until brave students challenged it, the law remained."

grammar.title: Connective Adverbs (Linking Words Between Sentences)
grammar.explanation: Connective adverbs link one complete sentence to the next instead of joining clauses inside a sentence. They usually open the new sentence and take a comma straight after them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
however shows contrast, like "but" across a full stop: "The rule seemed fair. However, it caused discrimination."
therefore shows a result, like "so" across a full stop: "The evidence was clear. Therefore, the rule was changed."
consequently shows a result and sounds more formal: "The traveller ignored the warning. Consequently, he was lost by dusk."
furthermore adds weight to the point before it: "The rule was unfair. Furthermore, it was incomplete."
in addition adds another point: "The rule caused disadvantage. In addition, it showed disregard for fairness."
meanwhile shows two things happening together: "Amal prepared her speech. Meanwhile, Sami organised the files."
on the other hand introduces the opposite view: "Some readers love adventure. On the other hand, others prefer realistic fiction."
unfortunately shows regret: "Unfortunately, many students were unaware of the rule."
fortunately shows relief: "Fortunately, the students decided to speak up."
as a result shows the consequence: "People protested. As a result, the law was reviewed."
grammar.commonMistake: Using "however" as though it were "but" creates one long run-on: "The legend was old however it was interesting." Split the ideas properly: "The legend was old. However, it was interesting."
grammar.memoryTip: Conjunctions work inside one sentence; connective adverbs reach across the full stop. If you can put a full stop before the linking word, it is an adverb and needs the comma after it.
grammar.practice: Part A. Choose the best connective adverb for each pair of sentences. | The students worked hard all week. ______, their debate was a great success. | The old files were full of stamps and long paragraphs. ______, some sections were illegible. | Nora believed the law was never meant to harm anyone. ______, Amal showed that it did. | ______, the power went out during the rainstorm. | The headteacher was impressed by the students. ______, she asked them to present at assembly. | Sami organised the timeline. ______, Amal prepared her closing speech. | Part B. Join each pair using the adverb in brackets, and punctuate it carefully. | The setting was a small village. The characters felt very real. (Furthermore) | Leo preferred legends. His sister always chose mysteries. (On the other hand) | The plot was confusing at first. Everything made sense at the end. (However) | The climber reached the top of the cliff. The rest of the group prepared a meal below. (Meanwhile) | Part C. Write two sentences about this unit and link them with "therefore" or "as a result". || Answer Key (for self-checking) — Part A: 1) Therefore / As a result, 2) Furthermore / In addition, 3) However, 4) Unfortunately, 5) Therefore / As a result, 6) Meanwhile. Part B: 1) "The setting was a small village. Furthermore, the characters felt very real." 2) "Leo preferred legends. On the other hand, his sister always chose mysteries." 3) "The plot was confusing at first. However, everything made sense at the end." 4) "The climber reached the top of the cliff. Meanwhile, the rest of the group prepared a meal below." Part C is open-ended — model answer: "This unit taught many connective words. Therefore, my writing now flows more smoothly between ideas."

grammar.title: Time Connectives for Storytelling
grammar.explanation: Time connectives tell the reader the order of events, so a retelling or a story opening stays easy to follow from beginning to end.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
First and Firstly open the sequence: "First, the children took their seats in the courthouse."
Then, Next and After that carry the middle: "Next, they searched the education files."
Meanwhile and At the same time show two events together: "Meanwhile, the rain hammered the windows."
Later and Eventually show that time has passed: "Eventually, the headteacher rose to speak."
Finally and In the end close the sequence: "Finally, Amal wrote in her journal."
Each of these openers takes a comma before the rest of the sentence.
Choose one opener per event, and never repeat "then" at the start of every line.
grammar.commonMistake: Beginning every event with "then" makes a retelling flat and hard to follow. Spread the openers out, and save "finally" for the last event only.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of five signposts along one road: First, Next, Meanwhile, Later, Finally. Plant each signpost once and the reader never gets lost.
grammar.practice: Part A. Put these five events from the story back into the right order. | The students held a school-wide debate. | The children acted out a trial in the courthouse. | Amal wrote in her journal about what she had learned. | The students found letters in a folder marked Unheard Voices. | The headteacher praised the students and read their slogan. | Part B. Rewrite your ordered list as one paragraph using first, then, after that, next and finally. | Part C. Add one sentence beginning with "Meanwhile" that shows something happening during the debate. || Answer Key (for self-checking) — Part A order: 1) The children acted out a trial in the courthouse. 2) The students found letters in a folder marked Unheard Voices. 3) The students held a school-wide debate. 4) The headteacher praised the students and read their slogan. 5) Amal wrote in her journal about what she had learned. Part B's exact wording is open, but it should follow that order — model paragraph: "First, the children acted out a trial in the courthouse. Next, the students found letters in a folder marked Unheard Voices. After that, the students held a school-wide debate. Then, the headteacher praised the students and read their slogan. Finally, Amal wrote in her journal about what she had learned." Part C is open-ended — model answer: "Meanwhile, the younger students in the audience listened closely and took notes."

grammar.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
grammar.explanation: Four connective mistakes turn up again and again in Grade 5 writing. Learn to spot each one and your sentences will hold together neatly.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Mistake 1 — opening formal writing with "And" or "But". Swap in a connective adverb.
"And they found more letters." becomes "Furthermore, they found more letters."
"But it was still unfair." becomes "However, it was still unfair."
In stories, opening with "And" or "But" is allowed for deliberate effect.
Mistake 2 — leaving the "because" clause on its own. "Because it rained." is unfinished.
Write "Because it rained, they worked inside." or "They worked inside because it rained."
Mistake 3 — swapping "but" and "so". But marks contrast: "The law helped, but it was incomplete."
So marks a result: "The law was incomplete, so they challenged it."
Mistake 4 — missing commas. Put one before FANBOYS joining two complete sentences, and one after a subordinate clause that comes first.
grammar.commonMistake: The commonest slip of all is the comma splice: "The mystery was solved, the detective found the final clue." Two complete sentences need a conjunction, a full stop or a semicolon between them, never a lone comma.
grammar.memoryTip: Read your work aloud and listen to the joins. Wherever your voice pauses but no linking word appears, that gap wants either a connective or a full stop.
grammar.practice: Part A. Rewrite each sentence correctly and say what was wrong with it. | Although the book was long and I could not stop reading. | The mystery was solved, the detective found the final clue. | However the legend was very old it was still interesting. | She wanted to read a fable. Because she liked animal stories. | Part B. Decide whether each gap needs "but" or "so". | The trial was only pretend, ______ the feelings were real. | The ink had faded, ______ the students could not read the file. | Part C. Write five sentences about a story you know. Use one coordinating conjunction, one subordinating conjunction and one connective adverb, then underline each connective. || Answer Key (for self-checking) — Part A: 1) "Although the book was long, I could not stop reading." (the "Although" clause was never closed off by a main clause — "and" kept it trapped as a fragment; swap "and" for a comma so a main clause follows). 2) "The mystery was solved because the detective found the final clue." (this was a comma splice — two complete sentences joined by a comma alone, with no conjunction). 3) "The legend was very old. However, it was still interesting." (a connective adverb was used mid-sentence like a conjunction with no punctuation, creating a run-on; it needs a full stop before it and a comma after). 4) "She wanted to read a fable because she liked animal stories." (the "Because..." clause was left standing alone as its own sentence, which is a fragment). Part B: 1) but, 2) so. Part C is open-ended — model answer: "Sami found the old files, and he read every page carefully. Because the ink had faded, he worked slowly. However, he finally found the folder marked Unheard Voices." (underlined connectives: and, Because, However).

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Genre Detective Game
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
One player describes a story without naming its genre, and the listener works the genre out from the clues.
Model lines for the speaker:
"My story is about a girl who finds a locked box under her bed."
"She follows three clues, and two of them turn out to be false."
"The setting stays the same, but the questions keep growing."
Model lines for the listener:
"I think this is a mystery, because you mentioned clues and false clues."
"The feature that helped me most was ______."
Play four rounds so that you cover four different genres, then swap roles.
After each round, agree on one feature the speaker could have made clearer.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With my adult helper listening, ask me to describe a story without naming its genre, then guess the genre and tell me which clue gave it away.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Book Recommendation Talk
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Prepare a talk of one to two minutes recommending one story to a friend. Cover five points in order.
Name the story and, if you know it, the author.
Say which genre it belongs to and give one feature that proves it.
Describe the main character and the setting without giving away the ending.
Explain why you enjoyed it and why your listener would enjoy it too.
Use at least two connectives to link your ideas.
Model lines:
"I recommend this book because the plot never stops moving."
"Although the beginning is slow, the story becomes very exciting in the middle."
"You would enjoy it, for you already love stories about brave journeys."
Practise once, then deliver it clearly and with real enthusiasm.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With my adult helper beside me, listen to my book recommendation and tell me whether my genre evidence convinced you.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Dramatic Reading
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose a short passage: either Teacher Yasmin's library tour or the courtroom scene from this unit.
Prepare it using four tools.
Pace: read exciting parts a little faster and thoughtful parts more slowly.
Volume: drop your voice for a whisper and lift it for a shout.
Pauses: a short pause before an important word builds suspense.
Voices: give each speaking character a slightly different tone.
Model lines to rehearse:
"Objection!" called Nora, the pretend prosecutor. (loud, quick)
"That is heartbreaking," whispered Nora. (quiet, slow)
Perform for a family member, then ask which moment felt most dramatic and why.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my dramatic reading with my adult helper present, and tell me where my pace or pausing helped the meaning most.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Group Story Starter
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work in a group of two to four. Agree on one genre before you begin.
The first speaker gives one or two opening sentences that fit the genre.
Model opening for adventure: "The boat rocked dangerously as the storm rolled in from the east."
Every speaker after that adds one or two sentences and must use at least one connective.
Model continuations:
"Meanwhile, the captain searched the horizon for land."
"Although the sail had torn, nobody turned back."
Go round the group five or six times, then agree together on a closing sentence.
Afterwards, discuss whether anyone drifted into a different genre, and list the connectives you used.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play the group story starter with me while my adult helper listens, and stop me if my sentence slips out of the genre we chose.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Prefix Expert Explains
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Teach the prefixes and endings from this unit to somebody at home, using six words of your own choice.
For each word, say three things in full sentences.
"The word is ______, and the base word inside it is ______."
"The prefix ______ changes the meaning to ______."
"Here is my own sentence: ______."
Then answer two questions about the word set.
"What do un-, dis- and in- all have in common?"
"Why does the prefix in- become il- in front of legible?"
Finish by explaining the difference between dissatisfied and uneasy in one clear sentence.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Three-Minute Unit Talk
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Plan and record a three-minute talk on this question: can young people really help change an unfair rule?
Structure your talk in four parts.
Opening: state your view in one clear sentence.
Idea one: use evidence from the courtroom story.

"However, one voice is rarely enough; the students needed letters, evidence and a debate."

writing.title: Writing 1: Plan and Write a Story Opening
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Plan and write the opening of your own story, in whichever genre you choose. Aim for 100 to 150 words.
Step 1. Choose your genre from the five on Teacher Yasmin's shelves.
Adventure: an exciting journey, a changing setting, danger to overcome.
Mystery: something puzzling, real clues, false clues, hidden answers.
Fable: animal characters who talk and behave like people, and one clear moral.
Legend: the distant past, one extraordinary deed, a traditional feel.
Realistic fiction: ordinary people, ordinary situations, feelings that ring true.
Step 2. Fill in the planning frame in notes, not full sentences.
Genre. Main character with name, age and one detail. Setting with time, weather and surroundings. Opening hook. Three connectives you will use.
Step 3. Write one or two paragraphs in the past tense.
Your first sentence must make the reader want the second one.
writing.modelText: The old wooden door of the school library creaked open, although nobody had pushed it. Amal froze at her desk. She had been the only person in the room since the final bell rang, and she was certain the caretaker had locked the corridor. However, there it was: the door wide open, letting in a draught that made her pages flutter. She stood up slowly because she did not want to make a sound. On the floor, just inside the doorway, lay a small folded note. While the rest of the school stood silent and empty, somebody had been here. Amal picked up the note and read three words that made her heart beat faster.
writing.sentenceStarter: The old wooden door creaked open, although...
writing.expectedLength: One to two paragraphs, 100 to 150 words

items: Genre: Mystery
Main character: Nadia, aged eleven, who always carries a notebook to write down anything strange she notices
Setting: a rainy Tuesday afternoon in the school's old art room, where dust covers every shelf
Opening hook: a locked cupboard that nobody remembers locking
Three connectives: however, meanwhile, finally

The art room smelled of turpentine and rain, and Nadia noticed the cupboard door was shut with a padlock nobody had ever used before. She tried the handle twice, however it would not budge. Meanwhile, the rest of the class filed out for lunch, leaving her alone with the strange silence of empty easels and dripping windows. She pressed her ear against the cold metal and heard, very faintly, something shift inside. Nobody had mentioned a new lock in the register, and the caretaker always left his keys on the same hook by the door. Finally, she spotted a torn corner of paper wedged beneath the cupboard, and she crouched down to read the words scratched across it.
otherAnswers: Any of the five genres works equally well — an adventure opening could instead begin mid-journey with a changing setting and a sudden danger.
A legend opening could start in the distant past with one extraordinary deed, such as a shepherd holding back a flood with only stones.
A realistic fiction opening could focus on an ordinary morning where one small, true-to-life feeling changes everything that follows.

writing.successCriteria: I chose one genre and showed its features; I introduced my character with one real detail; I described the setting; my first sentence hooks the reader; I used at least three different connectives; I wrote in the past tense throughout; I varied my sentence lengths.
writing.support: Reread the model opening and mark the five connectives in it before you plan your own.
writing.extension: Add one simile that fits your genre, in the way the story compares a drawing to a gavel's knock.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Journal Entry After the Debate
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write the journal entry of Amal, Sami or Nora on the evening after the school debate. Aim for 100 to 150 words.
Write in the first person and in the past tense.
Include three things.
One moment from the week that you cannot stop thinking about.
One feeling, and the reason behind it.
One thing you intend to do next.
Use at least two words from this unit, and at least two connectives.
writing.modelText: Tonight the courthouse still feels close, although we left it hours ago. I keep returning to the folder marked Unheard Voices. Those letters were not evidence to me; they were people. One student wrote that she felt punished for a condition she could not change, and I had to read the line twice. Unfortunately, nobody listened to her back then. Fortunately, we are listening now. I felt uncertain before the debate, because I did not know whether anyone would take three children seriously. However, the headteacher stood up at the end. Tomorrow I will start a letter of my own.
writing.sentenceStarter: Tonight the courthouse still feels close, although...

items: Moment I cannot stop thinking about: Tonight I keep picturing the moment the folder marked Unheard Voices finally opened, and the pages inside were so illegible that at first none of us could read a single line.
Feeling and reason: I felt a flash of injustice, because somebody had clearly wanted those letters never to be read again; however, tonight we finally read every word.
What I intend to do next: Tomorrow I intend to ask the librarian whether the school keeps any older records, so I can carry on where tonight left off.
otherAnswers: Writing as Amal instead of Sami would work just as well — for example, her moment could be the instant the headteacher stood up at the end of the debate.
Writing as Nora, the moment could instead be the silence in the room just before anyone was brave enough to speak first.
The chosen moment, feeling and next step are personal to the writer, so any true, specific detail from the week is a valid answer as long as the three required parts are all present.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote in the first person and past tense; I named one real moment from the story; I gave a feeling with its reason; I said what I would do next; I used two unit words and two connectives.
writing.support: Reread part 2 of the story and list three moments before you choose one to write about.
writing.extension: End with one short sentence of three words or fewer, so the entry closes with impact.

writing.title: Writing 3: Letter to the Headteacher
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a letter to the headteacher explaining why the students' civic education project mattered. Aim for 100 to 150 words.
Open with a greeting and say clearly why you are writing.
Give three reasons, each in its own sentence, and support one with evidence from the story.
Use at least three connectives, and make one of them a connective adverb.
Close with a request or a suggestion for next year.
Check your commas: before FANBOYS between two complete sentences, and after a subordinate clause that comes first.
writing.modelText: Dear Headteacher, I am writing about the civic education week that ended with our debate. The project mattered for three reasons. Firstly, we learned that a rule can be legal and still be unjust, because the file we read shut out students with a disability. Furthermore, we practised finding evidence rather than simply arguing louder. Although some records were illegible, we kept searching until the folder made everything clear. Finally, the week showed us that speaking together works. Therefore, I would like to ask that next year's class visits the courthouse too.
writing.sentenceStarter: Dear Headteacher, I am writing about...

items: Greeting and purpose: Dear Headteacher, I am writing to explain why our civic education project on fairness mattered so much to our class.
Reason one, with evidence: Firstly, the project showed us that a rule can be legal and still be unjust, because the file we studied excluded students with a disability from the swimming club.
Reason two: Furthermore, we learned to search for real evidence instead of simply arguing the loudest, even when some of the records were hard to read.
Reason three, with a connective adverb: Finally, the week proved that speaking together as a class carries more weight than speaking alone.
Closing request: Therefore, I would like to ask that next year's class visits the courthouse as well, so they can see the evidence for themselves.

writing.successCriteria: I opened with a greeting and a purpose; I gave three separate reasons; I supported one reason with evidence from the story; I used three connectives including one connective adverb; I closed with a request; my commas are in the right places.
writing.support: Draft your three reasons as short notes first, then decide which connective opens each one.
writing.extension: Rewrite your strongest reason twice, once with "because" and once with "therefore", and choose the better version.

writing.title: Writing 4: Design the Unfairness Poster
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Design a poster built around the slogan the students wrote: Unfairness, once noticed, must be challenged.
Plan the layout in notes before you write anything neatly.
Include the slogan in large letters at the top.
Give three reasons why speaking up matters, each in one short sentence.
Add one image idea and describe it in words for somebody who cannot see it.
Finish with one line telling the reader what to do first.
Keep every sentence short, since a poster is read from across the room.
writing.modelText: UNFAIRNESS, ONCE NOTICED, MUST BE CHALLENGED. Silence protects the rule, not the person. One voice starts the question; many voices finish it. Evidence turns an opinion into an argument. Image idea: a set of scales, tilted, with a single hand steadying the lighter side. Start today: write down what you saw, and tell one adult you trust.
writing.sentenceStarter: UNFAIRNESS, ONCE NOTICED, MUST BE CHALLENGED.
writing.expectedLength: One poster: slogan, three reasons, one image description, one call to action

items: Slogan, large letters at the top: UNFAIRNESS, ONCE NOTICED, MUST BE CHALLENGED.
Reason one: A quiet witness lets a rule stay wrong.
Reason two: Two voices convince faster than one voice repeats.
Reason three: A fact remembered is worth more than a feeling shouted.
Image description: a single candle lighting a row of unlit candles beside it.
Call to action: Notice something unfair? Write it down and tell your class teacher this week.
otherAnswers: Other true reasons work just as well, such as: A written record cannot be argued away, or A group asking together is harder to ignore.
The image can be any picture that carries the same idea in words, such as a single hand tipping a set of scales back level.
The call to action can be phrased differently as long as it gives one clear first step, such as: Seen something unfair? Tell a trusted adult today.

writing.successCriteria: My slogan is exact; I gave three different reasons; each sentence is short enough to read from a distance; I described an image in words; I ended with a clear first step.
writing.support: Say each reason aloud and cut any word the sentence can live without.
writing.extension: Write a second version of your call to action aimed at teachers rather than children.

writing.title: Writing 5: Use the Unit Words in a Story
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a paragraph of five to seven sentences about a character who meets an unfair situation.
Use at least six words from this unit's word list and underline each one.
Take your six words from more than one group, so you mix un-, dis-, in- and the -ible, -able or -ous endings.
Make the situation clear in your first sentence, and show how the character responds.
Check that every word you chose keeps its real meaning in your sentence.
writing.modelText: The notice on the gym door felt like an injustice from the moment Leo read it. Only pupils who had passed the swimming test could enter the new club, and the printing was so faded it was almost illegible. Leo felt uneasy, because the rule seemed to punish anyone who had started late. Unfortunately, the first three people he asked disregarded his question completely. He was not incapable of speaking up; he simply needed somebody to listen. Finally, he wrote out the whole problem and left it on the office desk.
writing.sentenceStarter: The notice on the gym door felt like an injustice when...
writing.expectedLength: One paragraph of five to seven sentences

items: Zara felt it was deeply unfair when the sports captain crossed her name off the relay team without any explanation.
She was unwilling to accept the decision without asking why, even though her friends discouraged her from making a fuss.
The captain seemed incapable of giving a clear reason, only mumbling that the list was final.
Zara stayed courageous and asked the PE teacher to check the selection sheet properly.
It turned out to be a sensible decision after all, since a genuine mistake had swapped her name with another Zara's.
By the end of the week, her place on the team was restored.
otherAnswers: Any character and unfair situation can work, and any six unit words from more than one group are acceptable as long as each keeps its true meaning — for example a story about a boy who is disbelieved when he reports a broken swing, using words like unnoticed, distrustful, invisible, incapable, furious and sensible.
The same situation could instead use a different six-word set from the same word list, provided the words still come from more than one group.

writing.successCriteria: I used six or more unit words and underlined them; my words came from more than one group; the unfair situation is clear by the end of sentence one; each word keeps its true meaning; I checked spelling and punctuation.
writing.support: Choose your six words first and write them in a list, then build the sentences around them.
writing.extension: Swap one word for a synonym and explain in one sentence which version is more precise.

writing.title: Writing 6: Peer Feedback and Revision
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Swap your Writing 1 story opening with a partner, then respond in writing to five questions.
Which genre has your partner written in, and how can you tell?
What is the strongest part of the opening?
Which two connectives did they use? Write them down.
Was anything confusing? Suggest one improvement.
Does the opening make you want to read on? Explain why.
Give your feedback as a sandwich: a strength, then a suggestion, then a second strength.
Finally, revise your own opening and write one sentence explaining what you changed and why.
writing.modelText: Your opening is clearly a mystery, because the missing key is never explained and you plant two false clues. The strongest part is the sound of the gate, which made me want to look over my shoulder. You used although and however. One suggestion: the second sentence tells me your character is frightened, but showing her shaking hands would be stronger. I would definitely read on, since you never reveal who moved the key. In my own revision, I replaced two ands with because and meanwhile, so the reasons are now clear.
writing.sentenceStarter: Your opening is clearly a ______, because...
writing.expectedLength: Five written responses plus one revision sentence

items: Genre and how I can tell: Your opening is clearly a legend, because it happens in the distant past and describes one extraordinary deed - the shepherd boy holding back the flood with only a wall of stones.
Strongest part: The strongest part is the image of the water rising past his knees while he kept stacking stones, because it makes the danger feel real.
Two connectives used: You used although and therefore.
Confusing point and suggestion: It was a little confusing that the village is never named; giving it a name would help me picture it more clearly.
Does it make me want to read on: Yes, I would definitely read on, because I still do not know whether the wall holds until morning.
My own revision and why: In my own revision, I replaced two short, choppy sentences with one sentence joined by although, so my opening now flows more smoothly and sounds less like a list.

writing.successCriteria: I answered all five questions in full sentences; my feedback was specific rather than general; I quoted two real connectives; my suggestion was kind and useful; I revised my own opening and explained the change.
writing.support: Point at the exact word or line you mean, so your partner knows where to look.

activities.title: Activities 1: Prefix and Suffix Sorting
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Sort all twenty-five unit words into four columns, then answer the question underneath.
Column 1 — words beginning with un-.
Column 2 — words beginning with dis-.
Column 3 — words beginning with in- (or its il- form).
Column 4 — words ending in -ible, -able or -ous.
Which column holds the most words? Write your answer in one full sentence.
Now write one sentence explaining what un-, dis- and in- all have in common.
activities.answerSummary: Ten un- words, six dis- words, five in- words and four words with special endings; illegible belongs with the endings because it carries both il- and -ible.

activities.title: Activities 2: Fill in the Prefix
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Add the correct prefix to complete each word. Choose from un-, dis-, in- and il-.
The puzzle was ______complete, so we could not finish it.
Many people were ______aware of the problem.
She felt ______satisfied with the unfair decision.
They showed ______regard for the feelings of others.
The old writing was ______legible because the ink had faded.
He felt ______capable of speaking in front of the whole school.
The journey into the forest was ______familiar and exciting.
______fortunately, the game was cancelled because of rain.
activities.answerSummary: The answers run in, un, dis, dis, il, in, un and Un; item 5 needs il- because in- changes form in front of the letter l.

activities.title: Activities 3: Match the Word to the Meaning
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Draw a line from each word to its meaning. Every meaning is used once.
Words: unrest, discrimination, invincible, monotonous, navigable.
Meanings: able to be travelled through; unable to be defeated; treating someone unfairly; very boring and always the same; unhappiness that may lead to protest.
Then choose the two words you found hardest and write one sentence for each.
activities.answerSummary: Unrest pairs with unhappiness that may lead to protest, discrimination with treating someone unfairly, invincible with unable to be defeated, monotonous with very boring and always the same, and navigable with able to be travelled through.

activities.title: Activities 4: Word Families
activities.instructionsAndItems:
For each word below, write the base word and then any other forms you can build from it.
discrimination — base word: ______ / other forms: ______
unfortunately — base word: ______ / other forms: ______
invincible — base word: ______ / other forms: ______
navigable — base word: ______ / other forms: ______
incomplete — base word: ______ / other forms: ______
Finish by writing one sentence that uses two words from the same family.
activities.answerSummary: Expected families are discriminate with discriminating, fortunate with fortune and fortunately, invincible with invincibility and invincibly (it has no shorter everyday base word — it comes from Latin vincere, to conquer), navigate with navigation and navigator, and complete with completely and completion.

activities.title: Activities 5: Genre Feature Grid
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Build a grid with five rows, one for each genre from the library tour.
Rows: adventure, mystery, fable, legend, realistic fiction.
Columns: typical characters, typical setting, what drives the plot, one clue that gives the genre away.
Fill every box using evidence from the two library tour passages.
Then answer this in one sentence: which two genres are easiest to confuse, and why?
activities.answerSummary: Adventure runs on journey and danger, mystery on clues and suspense, fables on talking animals and one moral, legends on the distant past and extraordinary deeds, and realistic fiction on ordinary people in ordinary situations; fable and legend are the easiest pair to confuse, because both are old and both are handed down.

activities.title: Activities 6: Language Feature Evidence Hunt
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Hunt through the courtroom story and copy out one example of each language feature.
A simile that compares using like or as.
A line of direct speech with correct punctuation.
A sentence that uses but to show contrast.
A sentence that uses because to give a reason.
A reporting clause such as she said or he answered.
A metaphor, where one thing is described as another.
For each one, write a second sentence explaining what the feature adds for the reader.
activities.answerSummary: Usable examples are the simile about the gavel's knock, the punctuated line from Nora, the contrast in the sentence about a legal but unjust law, the reason clause about people being unaware, the reporting clause said Amal, and the metaphor about the rule blocking hope.

assignments.title: A Different Type of Story learning portfolio
assignments.instructions: Submit two pieces. First, your Writing 1 story opening, revised after the partner feedback in Writing 6, with your three connectives underlined and your planning frame attached. Second, a recording of the Speaking 6 three-minute talk, with your written note of one strength and one improvement. The story opening earns full marks for ideas only when the genre is unmistakable from its features, and full marks for conventions only when every comma before FANBOYS and after a fronted subordinate clause is correct. The talk earns full marks for interaction only when the learner answers two follow-up questions with reasons.

quizzes.quizTitle: A Different Type of Story checkpoint
quizzes.question: What does the word "illegible" mean?
quizzes.options: Very boring because it is always the same. | Able to be travelled on, especially by boats. | Not awake and not aware of what is happening. | Hard to read or not clear enough to understand.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Hard to read or not clear enough to understand.

quizzes.question: Which prefix turns "complete" into a word meaning the opposite?
quizzes.explanation: In- means not, so complete becomes incomplete; -ous and -able are endings, and re- means again.

quizzes.question: Teacher Yasmin says one genre is built on suspense, real clues and false clues. Which genre is it?

quizzes.quizTitle: A Different Type of Story checkpoint

teacherNotes.note: Pre-teach discrimination, injustice and disability before the courtroom story, and say plainly that the unfair rule in it is wrong. Some learners in the room may have a disability themselves or in the family, so name the rule as the problem and never the person, and allow anyone to step out of the discussion. An adult must sit with the learner for every AI tutor task and every recording; no child is left alone with the device, and recordings stay inside the class space. Give feedback on three things: complete sentences, quoted evidence rather than opinion, and comma placement around connectives.

teacherNotes.noteType: Grammar answer key and tutor guidance
teacherNotes.note: Grammar answers, teacher copy. Grammar 2 Part A: but, or, yet, for, nor, but (and is acceptable), for. Part B: but, or, yet, so, and. Part C: only the mystery-or-legend question and the food-and-water sentence need no comma, because neither joins two complete sentences. Grammar 3 Part A: When or After, because, Although or Even though, because, If or When, until, Before, until. Part B: If, until, Although, while or when, unless, After or When, because or since. Grammar 4 Part A: As a result or Therefore, Furthermore or In addition, However, Unfortunately, Therefore or As a result, Meanwhile. Grammar 5 Part A order: trial, letters, debate, headteacher, journal. Grammar 6 Part B: but, so. Tutor guidance: the most useful requests are asking the tutor to compare a legend with a fable, to explain why in- becomes il- before legible, and to test the learner on six prefix words. Every one of these is done with an adult sitting alongside.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Column counts are ten un- words, six dis- words, five in- words and four words with special endings, so the un- column is the largest. Illegible is the tricky one: it carries the il- form of in- and the -ible ending, and either column is acceptable if the learner explains the choice. The shared idea is that un-, dis- and in- all reverse the meaning of the base word.

The prefixes run: 1 in (incomplete), 2 un (unaware), 3 dis (dissatisfied), 4 dis (disregard), 5 il (illegible), 6 in (incapable), 7 un (unfamiliar), 8 Un (Unfortunately). Item 5 is the teaching point: in- shifts to il- before the letter l because inlegible is awkward to say. Item 8 needs a capital letter, since it opens the sentence.

The pairs are unrest with unhappiness that may lead to protest, discrimination with treating someone unfairly, invincible with unable to be defeated, monotonous with very boring and always the same, and navigable with able to be travelled through. Learners most often swap unrest and discrimination, so ask them to point at the base word inside each one.

Accept discriminate and discriminating; fortunate, fortune and fortunately; invincibility (vincible is rare and need not be produced); navigate, navigation and navigator; complete, completely and completion. Give the mark for any real related form, but check the spelling of the base word rather than the number of forms offered.

Adventure needs journey, changing setting and danger; mystery needs a puzzle, clues and suspense; fable needs talking animals and one moral; legend needs the distant past and an extraordinary deed; realistic fiction needs ordinary people in believable situations. The expected confusion is fable with legend, because both are old and handed down, but only the fable must end with a moral.

Accept these from the story: the simile "as clear as a gavel's knock" or "as navigable as a city map"; direct speech such as "Objection!" called Nora; the contrast in "It may have been legal, but it was not just"; the reason in "Because many people were unaware of its effects"; the reporting clause "said Amal" or "answered Sami"; and the metaphor "It blocked hope". Award the second mark only when the learner explains the effect, not just the label.

Correct: hard to read or not clear enough to understand. Legible means readable, and il- reverses it. If a learner picks the boats option they have confused illegible with navigable, so send them back to the -ible and -able group.
Correct: in-. Complete becomes incomplete. Watch for learners choosing -ous or -able: those are endings, not prefixes, and re- would give recomplete, which is not an English word.
Correct: mystery. The clue words in the stem are suspense and false clues, both of which belong to the dark blue shelf. A learner who answers adventure has heard excitement rather than puzzle.
Correct: fable. Two conditions must both hold, talking animals and a moral. Legend is the near miss, so ask the learner which of the two always ends with a lesson.

Correct: The trial began, and the room grew quiet. Both halves could stand alone as sentences, so the comma sits before and. The other three options place the comma after the conjunction or inside a clause.

Correct: unrest. The phrase civil unrest describes public unhappiness that may become protest. Unique and uneasy do not follow the word civil, and unfortunately is an adverb, so it cannot fill a noun slot.
Correct: uneasy. Amal lists three feelings, so the missing word must describe how a student felt. Unexpected and unfamiliar describe events and places rather than feelings.
Correct: uncertain. Nora is explaining why people stayed silent: they were not sure enough to speak. Unaware would mean they did not know at all, which contradicts the sentence before it.

Correct: yet. The second clause surprises the reader after the first, which is exactly the job of yet. So would also make sense in meaning but is not offered; nor needs a negative first clause, and or needs a choice.

Correct: linking two separate sentences to show contrast. However is a connective adverb, which is why a full stop precedes it and a comma follows it. Anyone choosing the first option has confused it with a conjunction such as but.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "A Different Type of Story" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 9-10 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'unrest'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Identify and compare the five story genres in this unit and describe the features of each.
Support inferences about characters, viewpoint and language choices with evidence from the text.
Work out the meaning of longer words from the prefixes un-, dis-, in- and the endings -ible, -able and -ous.
Join ideas with coordinating conjunctions, subordinating conjunctions and connective adverbs, punctuated correctly.
Plan, draft and revise a story opening of 100 to 150 words in a genre of your choice.
Recommend, perform and discuss stories aloud, then reflect on what made the talk effective.

sections.title: Words They Will Learn
items: Words with the Prefix un- (meaning 'not' or 'the opposite of'): unrest · uneasy · unexpected · unsuccessful · unfamiliar · uncertain · unaware · unconscious · unique · unfortunately
Words with the Prefix dis- (meaning 'not', 'opposite of', or 'remove'): dissatisfied · disadvantage · disability · disregard · discrimination · dismantle
Words with the Prefix in- (meaning 'not'): incomplete · injustice · incapable · incompetent · invincible
Words with Special Endings (-ible / -able / -ous): illegible · navigable · miraculous · monotonous

sections.title: This Unit's Texts
items: Unit reading — "The Library Tour: Adventure and Mystery"
Close reading — "The Library Tour: Fable, Legend and Realistic Fiction"
Story — "The Case of the Incomplete Rule, part 1"
Story — "The Case of the Incomplete Rule, part 2"

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "The Library Tour: Adventure and Mystery" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Case of the Incomplete Rule, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "What Are Connectives and Conjunctions?" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
items: Connectives glue ideas together so the reader can follow your thinking.
They worked hard, for they believed in justice.
They protested because the rule was unfair.
The rule seemed fair. However, it caused discrimination.
First, the children took their seats in the courthouse.
Furthermore, they found more letters.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:
items: The genre feature grid in Activities 5 completed accurately, plus five genres named in the Speaking 1 detective game.
Six quoted details recorded in Activities 6, plus two-mark evidence answers in the Story and inference comprehension section.
All twenty-five words sorted correctly in Activities 1, and the word-family table in Activities 4 completed.
Grammar practices 2, 3 and 4 completed, with commas placed correctly in at least eight of the ten joined sentences.
The Writing 1 planning frame and draft, with at least three different connectives underlined and a revision made after feedback.
The recorded Speaking 6 three-minute talk, plus a written reflection naming one strength and one improvement.
